Toil
TOYL
n. (hard and continued labor, especially such as fatigues body or mind)
From Old French toiler, to drag about, entangle, ultimately from Latin tudicula, a machine for crushing olives. The word carries in its root the picture of something wrung out under pressure, not merely worked at.

Biblical Definition

Genesis names toil at both ends of a life. Lamech, naming his son Noah, looks forward to relief from it — this same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed — and the toil he means is the ground's own curse from Eden, the sweat of the brow that now attends every harvest. Joseph, decades later in Egypt, names his firstborn Manasseh, Forgetting, because God hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house — the toil there is not the ground's curse but the specific grief of the pit and Potiphar's house, the years a man spends before the LORD turns his captivity.

Between Lamech's hope and Joseph's relief sits the ordinary toil Ecclesiastes examines at length: what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun? The Preacher's answer is not that toil is meaningless in itself but that toil pursued as its own reward, without reference to the God who gives the appetite to enjoy its fruit, dissolves into vexation. Christ's invitation stands against all three uses at once — Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest — not a promise that toil ends in this life, but that the curse's full weight need not be carried alone.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): labor with pain and fatigue; hard work that exhausts the strength, either of body or mind.

expand to see more

TOIL, n. Labor attended with fatigue and pain; hard work that wearies the body or mind.

LABOUR, n. Exertion of body or mind for the attainment of some object, especially when severe or continued.

CURSE, n. Malediction; a solemn or invocatory imprecation of evil; the sentence pronounced upon the ground for man's sin.

VEXATION, n. The act of vexing, or the state of being vexed; disquiet; agitation of mind; trouble.

REST, n. Cessation of labor or motion; repose; quiet; freedom from toil, disturbance, or pain.

Key Scripture

Gen 5:29 — "And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed."

Gen 41:51 — "And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house."

Ecc 2:22 — "For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun?"

Mat 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Modern Corruption

Toil is sold either as pure curse to be escaped or pure virtue to be maximized, when Scripture treats it as a real burden from the fall that God Himself proposes to carry with a man, not merely to end.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, but it does face two opposite temptations, both older than any modern movement. One treats toil as an unmixed evil, something a righteous life should aim to escape as fully and as soon as possible. The other treats ceaseless toil itself as the mark of a well-lived life, as though the curse on the ground were actually a virtue to be pursued for its own sake.

Genesis will not allow either. The toil Lamech names is a real curse on a real ground, worth naming as a curse and worth hoping for relief from; the toil Joseph names is real grief God used and then, in His time, caused him to forget. Ecclesiastes' vexation is not toil as such but toil cut loose from the God who gives a man the ability to enjoy what his hands produce. Christ's rest is offered to the toiling and heavy laden precisely as toiling and heavy laden — not a call to stop working, but an invitation to stop carrying the curse's weight alone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew itstsabown (H6093), toil, labor, sorrow; the word of the ground's curse in Genesis 3:17 and 5:29, and again of Joseph's own toil in Genesis 41:51.

expand to see more

Hebrew itstsabown (H6093) — toil, sorrow, labor; the very word pronounced over the ground in Genesis 3:17, echoed in 5:29 and 41:51.

Hebrew amal (H5999) — labor, toil, travail; the Preacher's own word for the vexation of Ecclesiastes 2:22.

Hebrew nacham (H5162) — to comfort, to console; the verb behind Noah's very name and Lamech's hope in Genesis 5:29.

Hebrew nashah (H5382, root of Manasseh) — to forget, to cause to forget; Joseph's own naming-word in Genesis 41:51.

Greek kopiao (G2872) — to grow weary with labor, to toil; the verb behind “labour” in Christ's invitation, Matthew 11:28.

Usage

"“this same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands” — Lamech's hope at Noah's birth."

"“God hath made me forget all my toil” — Joseph's naming of Manasseh."

"“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” — Christ's answer to toil itself."
